newsitem.title: UK: UK to study 3 models for London Underground sale.
newsitem.headline: UK to study 3 models for London Underground sale.

text.p: Britain's Transport Secretary Sir George Young said the government would examine three options for privatising the London Underground (LU) rail network.
-- selling LU as a single business.
-- selling or franchising lines or groups of lines to different operators who would be responsible for stations, track and trains on each line or group of lines.
-- privatising it along the lines of British Rail, with a track authority (similar to Railtrack) and franchisees running trains on individual lines or groups of lines.
Young, who said the government had no favoured option, told parliament that he would publish a policy white paper in the summer examining the three alternatives.
"The government has concluded that privatisation is the right way forward," he said.

He said he hoped privatisation would lead to core investment of around 750 million stg a year -- approximately the maximum that LU estimates is sensible and 50 percent more than has been achieved so far in the 1990s.
"I do not believe that this rate of progress would be possible if LU were to remain in the public sector," he said.
Young assured MPs that the "tube" would remain a fully integrated network following privatisation, with through ticketing and freedom of interchange.
Season tickets would be explictly safeguarded and current concessionary fares would be unaffected, as would employees' pensions rights and travel concessions, he added.
Young said the government would seek ways of encouraging employees and passengers to acquire shares in the privatised Underground.

As with the privatisation of the national rail network, the government will require private operators to provide a guaranteed minimum level of service, broadly safeguarding the existing level of services.

After recycling privatisation proceeds into working off the tube's 1.2 billion stg investment backlog within five years, the majority of any remaining surplus will be channelled into extra support for LU or for transport investment elsehwere.
The main opposition Labour party reiterated its hostility to the planned sell-off, with transport spokesman Andrew Smith calling Young's proposals "half-baked".
"What makes him think it is going to work when he cannot even tell us how he is going to do it?" he asked.

If it wins the coming election, Labour would explore ways of attracting private finance to LU but would keep it under public control. Young's proposed "white paper" would thus never see the light of day.
